title: What is an MIS, really?
audience: Nonprofit programme leaders and M&E heads who have bought software but still fight over report numbers
learning_outcome: The viewer can explain the mechanism by which separate team records produce conflicting reports, and name the five layers of an MIS that prevent it.

voice.persona: A warm, curious female narrator in her thirties with a light Indian English accent. Clear, conversational, like a favourite teacher explaining something she finds genuinely fascinating.

claims.claim: Sitara Foundation, Kavya, and every number shown (500 rows, 37 duplicates, 463 people, 298 placed, 120 hours)
A dashboard without a decision is decoration
MAP: Model, Align, Power with AI

scenes.notes: Curiosity gap + stakes. Mystery framing. Title lands only at the end.
scenes.visual: Dark-to-cream: open on a dim ink background with a single clock reading 9:59 → 10:00 (tick). A phone-call card slides in: 'Funder call' with a question bubble typed out: 'How many learners did you place this quarter?'. Then three team avatars (simple circles with Programme coral / M&E yellow / Finance teal) each pop a big number bubble 312, 287, 341 on b4/b5/b6, slightly overlapping, each with a pop. b7: the three numbers line up and a thin red question line connects them. b8: big '?' fades. b9: all three numbers shake once and dim. b10: kinetic title: 'What is an MIS,' then 'really?' in deep coral, with the starburst accent.

beats.text: Tomorrow. Ten a.m.

voice.direction: Low, intriguing, unhurried. Setting a scene.

beats.text: Your biggest funder asks you one simple question.
How many learners did you place this quarter?

voice.direction: Asking the question as the funder would, curious and direct.

beats.text: Programme says 312.
beats.say: Programme says three hundred and twelve.

beats.text: M&E says 287.
beats.say: And M and E? Two eighty-seven.

beats.text: Finance says 341.
Same organisation. Same quarter. Three answers.

voice.direction: Slow and deliberate, each phrase landing.

beats.text: So who got it wrong?

voice.direction: Playful, inviting the viewer to guess.

beats.text: Nobody. And that's exactly the problem.

voice.direction: A beat of surprise, then a firm, warm punchline.

beats.text: Let's find out why. What is an MIS, really?

voice.direction: Bright and inviting, the start of a story.

scenes.chapter: A hospital you'd walk out of
scenes.notes: Anchor the abstract problem to a familiar, emotionally loaded situation, then map it back.
scenes.visual: Flat, friendly illustration style (simple geometric people: circle head + rounded body, no faces needed). Centre: a patient bed icon labelled 'One patient'. b2: three figures appear around it — Doctor, Nurse, Pharmacist — each holding its own folder (folder icons in three colours). b3: the doctor's folder updates: a line 'Dose: 5mg → 10mg' animates in the doctor's folder only (with a little pen stroke). b4: a dashed arrow tries to travel to the pharmacist's folder and stops halfway with a small ✕; pharmacist folder still says 'Dose: 5mg' — highlight in danger red. b5: a subtle 'EXIT' sign glows top-right (wry joke). b6: the MAPPING moment — each label morphs: 'One patient' → 'One learner', 'Doctor' → 'Programme', 'Nurse' → 'M&E', 'Pharmacist' → 'Finance'; the bed icon morphs into a student/graduation-cap icon; folders become spreadsheet icons. Use a smooth crossfade + slide for each label, staggered on the words in b6. b7: zoom out slightly; caption-style title 'Most nonprofits run like this hospital' with 'this hospital' in coral.

beats.text: Picture a hospital. One patient.
The doctor keeps a file. The nurse keeps her own file. The pharmacist keeps a third.
On Monday, the doctor doubles the dose.
The pharmacist's file never hears about it.
You'd walk out of that hospital, wouldn't you?

voice.direction: Wry, a hint of a smile.

beats.text: Now swap the words. The patient becomes a learner. The doctor becomes your programme team. The pharmacist becomes finance.
Most nonprofits run exactly like this hospital. Not because anyone is careless, but because nobody designed it any other way.

scenes.notes: Show the mechanism of failure, live. The time-lapse should feel like watching a slow-motion accident.
scenes.visual: Layout: left column = 'the field' (a learner avatar 'Kavya', a field officer with a phone, a trainer with a clipboard). Right = three spreadsheet panels stacked or side by side: Programme (coral header), M&E (yellow), Finance (teal), each with a few rows. Top-centre: a week clock / calendar strip 'Week 1 ... Week 13'. Top-right corner: an hours counter 'Hours spent reconciling: 0'. Org label 'Sitara Foundation · fictional · 500 learners' and ILLUSTRATIVE DATA tag. b1: org label + field + empty sheets appear. b2: Week 1 highlights; an event token (small rounded pill 'Enrolled') flies from the phone along a curved path into Programme sheet only, creating row 'Kavya Sharma'. b3: Week 2; a paper icon from the trainer → waits → flies into M&E sheet a beat later, creating row 'K. Sharma'. b4: Week 3; a '₹ stipend' token flies into Finance creating 'Kavya S.'. Highlight the three Kavya rows with yellow outline and thin dashed connectors between them labelled 'same person?'. b5: TIME-LAPSE: the week strip races Week 4 → Week 13; dozens of tokens (many colours) fly from the field into random single sheets; sheets fill up with rows (scrolling); hours counter starts climbing. b6: some rows flash red as values diverge (e.g. 'Placed' vs 'Training'); show drift with little ≠ marks between panels. b7: hours counter rolls 0 → 40 → 80 → 120 in sync with the words; counter grows in size each step. b8: time-lapse stops at Week 13; zoom on the three Kavya rows, which now show three different statuses: Placed / Training / Stipend stopped. Hold.

beats.text: Let's watch it happen. Meet Sitara Foundation, a fictional skilling nonprofit with five hundred learners.
Week one. Kavya enrols. The field officer adds her to the programme sheet.
Week two. Her trainer marks attendance on paper. A week later, someone in M&E types it in again, as K. Sharma.
Week three. Finance pays her stipend. Only finance knows, and to them she's Kavya S.
Now multiply Kavya by five hundred, and run the clock for a whole quarter.

voice.direction: Energy rising, like starting a race.

beats.say: Now multiply Kaavya by five hundred. And run the clock, for the entire quarter.

beats.text: Every event lands in one sheet, but not the others. Copies drift. Spellings multiply.
And quietly, a counter keeps climbing. Hours spent copying and reconciling. Forty. Eighty. A hundred and twenty.
By the end of the quarter, Kavya lives in three places, and none of them agree.

scenes.notes: Prediction makes the reveal memorable. Give real silence for the countdown.
scenes.visual: Direct address. b1: a large 'Your turn' kicker. b2: three tall choice cards (Programme 312 coral, M&E 287 yellow, Finance 341 teal) with a subtle hover-like float. b3: a circular countdown ring in the centre counts 3 → 2 → 1 over the pause (the beat's pause is 2.6 s), with each number scaling in; ticking sfx. b4: ring completes, cards gently pulse, text 'Hold that thought.'

beats.text: So here's a question for you.

voice.direction: Direct, turning to the viewer, warm.

beats.text: If you had to send the funder one number tonight, which would you pick? Programme, M&E, or finance?
Take three seconds.
Got one? Good. Hold on to it.
beats.say: Got one? Good. Now hold on to it.

scenes.notes: Based on experiments/hyperframes/index.html, re-timed to the beats. Surprise, then reframe the misconception that someone made an error.
scenes.visual: Reuse and adapt the experiment composition: b1 three team cards top. b2: 500-row grid appears with counter '500 rows'. b3: 37 duplicate rows glow yellow and fly to their twins; the Kavya cluster (Kavya Sharma / Kavya S. / K. Sharma) merges into one chip. b4: counter rolls 500 → 463 'real people'. b5: grid dims except placed rows which turn coral. b6: '298' rolls up huge in coral, label 'actually placed'; team cards strike through. b7: hold, small text 'Not 312. Not 287. Not 341.' b8: closing line 'Each team counted correctly. They were counting different things.' with the second sentence in italic coral.

beats.text: Here's what actually happened.

voice.direction: Lowered voice, like revealing a secret.

beats.text: Line up all three sheets and you get five hundred rows.
But thirty-seven of them are the same people, typed twice and spelled differently.
Merge them, and five hundred rows become four hundred and sixty-three real people.
Now count who was actually placed.
Two hundred and ninety-eight.

voice.direction: The big reveal, bright and emphatic.

beats.text: None of the three numbers was right.
And here's the twist. Each team counted correctly. They were just counting different things.

voice.direction: Thoughtful insight, slowing on the last sentence.

scenes.chapter: Building an MIS, floor by floor
scenes.notes: Each floor answers a failure the viewer has just seen. The definition is earned, then stated.
scenes.visual: A building/stack metaphor centre-left: five horizontal floors stack from the bottom up, each a wide rounded slab with a number badge, an icon and a short label. Right side: a 'what it fixes' panel that shows a tiny callback to the problem from earlier scenes for each floor. Floor 1 (coral) 'One ID per person' — callback: three Kavya chips merge into one 'Kavya Sharma · ID 0217'. Floor 2 (teal) 'One place per event' — callback: four event tokens (Enrolled, Attended, Stipend, Placed) drop into a single record card. Floor 3 (yellow) 'Shared rules' — callback: a rule chip 'Placed = job offer + joined' and a blocked action 'Placed before trained ✕'. Floor 4 (teal) 'A view for every team' — callback: three small screens labelled Programme / M&E / Finance, all wired to one record. Floor 5 (coral, glowing) 'A loop back to the field' — callback: a phone notification slides in: 'Kavya missed 3 sessions. Call her today.' with a ping. b8: the five floors pulse in sequence bottom to top; a bracket labelled 'MIS' wraps them. b9: definition card replaces the right panel: 'One record per person, shared by everyone, that the work runs through.' with 'that the work runs through' in coral. Each floor rises in with a soft thud.

beats.text: So what would fix this? Not a better spreadsheet. A different kind of system.
Let's build it, one floor at a time.
Floor one. One ID per person. Kavya gets one record, and only one.
Floor two. One place to record each event. Enrolment, attendance, stipend, placement. Entered once, where the work happens.
Floor three. Shared rules. Placed means the same thing to everyone, and the system won't let you mark someone placed before they've trained.

voice.direction: Clear, slightly firm on the rule.

beats.text: Floor four. A view for every team. Programme, M&E and finance each see their own screen, all drawing from the same record.
Floor five, the one most people miss. The data flows back to the field. Kavya has missed three sessions. Call her today.

voice.direction: Leaning in, this is the important one; warm urgency on the last sentence.

beats.text: Put those five floors together, and you have a management information system.
One record per person, shared by everyone, that the work actually runs through.

voice.direction: Slow, warm, definitive. The line to remember.

scenes.notes: Before/after on the same events makes the difference undeniable.
scenes.visual: Split screen with a soft vertical divider. Left header 'Without an MIS' (grey), right header 'With an MIS' (coral). Both sides share the same week strip at top. b1: headers + week strip appear. b2: left side: the familiar three sheets with tokens flying into single sheets and rows going out of sync (re-use quarter-sim style, faster). b3: right side: the same coloured tokens fly into ONE central record card (Kavya Sharma · ID 0217) whose timeline fills: Enrolled ✓ Attended ✓ Stipend ✓ Placed ✓; also three small team screens below light up together. b4: bottom of each side: report counter. Left shows three flickering numbers 312/287/341; right shows a single steady '298' for all three teams. b5: right side gets a small stopwatch '2 min' and a pill '120 hours back to learners' in teal.

beats.text: Now let's replay that same quarter. Same learners, same events, but with an MIS.
On the left, the old way. Three sheets, three versions.
On the right, every event lands in one record, the moment it happens.
At the end of the quarter, everyone sees the same number. Two hundred and ninety-eight.

voice.direction: Calm confidence, emphasis on the number.

beats.text: The funder call takes two minutes, and those hundred and twenty hours go back to the learners.

scenes.chapter: What an MIS is not, and Monday's questions
scenes.notes: Fast myth-busting, then transfer to the viewer's own organisation.
scenes.visual: Part A (b1–b4): heading 'An MIS is not…'. Three cards stack vertically and each gets a hand-drawn coral strike-through on its beat: 'Software you buy' (sub: 'Software is a tool. The system is how you agree to work.'), 'A dashboard' (sub: 'A dashboard without a decision is decoration.'), 'A bigger spreadsheet' (sub: 'More columns won't fix three copies.'). Part B (b5–b8): cards slide away; a notepad / clipboard titled 'Ask your team on Monday' with three numbered questions writing themselves in (typewriter or handwritten reveal), each with a checkbox that ticks: 1 'How many places does one learner live?' 2 'Who decides what "placed" means?' 3 'Does data come back to the field?'.

beats.text: Before we finish, three things an MIS is not.
It's not software you buy. Software is a tool. The system is how your organisation agrees to work.
It's not a dashboard. A dashboard without a decision is decoration.
And it's not a bigger spreadsheet. More columns won't fix three copies.
So here are three questions to ask your team on Monday.
One. How many places does one learner live?
Two. Who decides what placed means?
Three. Does the data ever come back to the people in the field?

scenes.notes: MAP in one breath, brand sign-off, next episode.
scenes.visual: b1: three MAP chips appear in sequence on the words Model (coral), Align (teal), Power (yellow), each with its 3–5 word line underneath, then compress upward. Then the EdZola hand-drawn wordmark (assets/brand/edzola-wordmark-transparent.png) draws/fades in centre with tagline 'Systems built for the world's hardest work.' and the floral mark rotating slowly. b2: 'Next episode' peach card slides up: 'Why 80% placement isn't the same as 80% employment'.

beats.text: At EdZola, we build these systems in three moves. Model what's worth knowing. Align it with how people actually work. And power it with AI, once the data can be trusted.

voice.direction: Warm and assured, a closing thought.

beats.text: Next time: why an eighty percent placement rate might not mean what you think.

voice.direction: Teasing, curious, leaving them wanting more.
